223 |     .. [4] Predicting Good Probabilities with Supervised Learning,
224 |            A. Niculescu-Mizil & R. Caruana, ICML 2005
225 |     """
226 | 
227 |     def __init__(
228 |         self,
229 |         base_estimator=None,
230 |         *,
231 |         method="sigmoid",
232 |         cv=None,
233 |         n_jobs=None,
234 |         ensemble=True,
235 |     ):
236 |         self.base_estimator = base_estimator
237 |         self.method = method
238 |         self.cv = cv
239 |         self.n_jobs = n_jobs
240 |         self.ensemble = ensemble
241 | 
242 |     def fit(self, X, y, sample_weight=None):
243 |         """Fit the calibrated model.
244 | 
245 |         Parameters
246 |         ----------
247 |         X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
248 |             Training data.
249 | 
250 |         y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
251 |             Target values.
252 | 
253 |         sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
254 |             Sample weights. If None, then samples are equally weighted.
255 | 
256 |         Returns
257 |         -------
258 |         self : object
259 |             Returns an instance of self.
260 |         """
261 |         check_classification_targets(y)
262 |         X, y = indexable(X, y)
263 | 
264 |         if self.base_estimator is None:
265 |             # we want all classifiers that don't expose a random_state
266 |             # to be deterministic (and we don't want to expose this one).
267 |             base_estimator = LinearSVC(random_state=0)
268 |         else:
269 |             base_estimator = self.base_estimator
270 | 
271 |         self.calibrated_classifiers_ = []
272 |         if self.cv == "prefit":
273 |             # `classes_` should be consistent with that of base_estimator
274 |             check_is_fitted(self.base_estimator, attributes=["classes_"])
275 |             self.classes_ = self.base_estimator.classes_
276 | 
277 |             pred_method, method_name = _get_prediction_method(base_estimator)
278 |             n_classes = len(self.classes_)
279 |             predictions = _compute_predictions(pred_method, method_name, X, n_classes)
280 | 
281 |             calibrated_classifier = _fit_calibrator(
282 |                 base_estimator,
283 |                 predictions,
284 |                 y,
285 |                 self.classes_,
286 |                 self.method,
287 |                 sample_weight,
288 |             )
289 |             self.calibrated_classifiers_.append(calibrated_classifier)
290 |         else:
291 |             # Set `classes_` using all `y`
292 |             label_encoder_ = LabelEncoder().fit(y)
293 |             self.classes_ = label_encoder_.classes_
294 |             n_classes = len(self.classes_)
295 | 
296 |             # sample_weight checks
297 |             fit_parameters = signature(base_estimator.fit).parameters
298 |             supports_sw = "sample_weight" in fit_parameters
299 |             if sample_weight is not None:
300 |                 sample_weight = _check_sample_weight(sample_weight, X)
301 |                 if not supports_sw:
302 |                     estimator_name = type(base_estimator).__name__
303 |                     warnings.warn(
304 |                         f"Since {estimator_name} does not support "
305 |                         "sample_weights, sample weights will only be"
306 |                         " used for the calibration itself."
307 |                     )
308 | 
309 |             # Check that each cross-validation fold can have at least one
310 |             # example per class
311 |             if isinstance(self.cv, int):
312 |                 n_folds = self.cv
313 |             elif hasattr(self.cv, "n_splits"):
314 |                 n_folds = self.cv.n_splits
315 |             else:
316 |                 n_folds = None
317 |             if n_folds and np.any(
318 |                 [np.sum(y == class_) < n_folds for class_ in self.classes_]
319 |             ):
320 |                 raise ValueError(
321 |                     f"Requesting {n_folds}-fold "
322 |                     "cross-validation but provided less than "
323 |                     f"{n_folds} examples for at least one class."
324 |                 )
325 |             cv = check_cv(self.cv, y, classifier=True)
326 | 
327 |             if self.ensemble:
328 |                 parallel = Parallel(n_jobs=self.n_jobs)
329 | 
330 |                 self.calibrated_classifiers_ = parallel(
331 |                     delayed(_fit_classifier_calibrator_pair)(
332 |                         clone(base_estimator),
333 |                         X,
334 |                         y,
335 |                         train=train,
336 |                         test=test,
337 |                         method=self.method,
338 |                         classes=self.classes_,
339 |                         supports_sw=supports_sw,
340 |                         sample_weight=sample_weight,
341 |                     )
342 |                     for train, test in cv.split(X, y)
343 |                 )
344 |             else:
345 |                 this_estimator = clone(base_estimator)
346 |                 _, method_name = _get_prediction_method(this_estimator)
347 |                 pred_method = partial(
348 |                     cross_val_predict,
349 |                     estimator=this_estimator,
350 |                     X=X,
351 |                     y=y,
352 |                     cv=cv,
353 |                     method=method_name,
354 |                     n_jobs=self.n_jobs,
355 |                 )
356 |                 predictions = _compute_predictions(
357 |                     pred_method, method_name, X, n_classes
358 |                 )
359 | 
360 |                 if sample_weight is not None and supports_sw:
361 |                     this_estimator.fit(X, y, sample_weight)
362 |                 else:
363 |                     this_estimator.fit(X, y)
364 |                 calibrated_classifier = _fit_calibrator(
365 |                     this_estimator,
366 |                     predictions,
367 |                     y,
368 |                     self.classes_,
369 |                     self.method,
370 |                     sample_weight,
371 |                 )
372 |                 self.calibrated_classifiers_.append(calibrated_classifier)
373 | 
374 |         first_clf = self.calibrated_classifiers_[0].base_estimator
375 |         if hasattr(first_clf, "n_features_in_"):
376 |             self.n_features_in_ = first_clf.n_features_in_
377 |         if hasattr(first_clf, "feature_names_in_"):
378 |             self.feature_names_in_ = first_clf.feature_names_in_
379 |         return self
380 | 
381 |     def predict_proba(self, X):
382 |         """Calibrated probabilities of classification.
383 | 
384 |         This function returns calibrated probabilities of classification
385 |         according to each class on an array of test vectors X.
386 | 
387 |         Parameters
388 |         ----------
389 |         X : The samples, as accepted by base_estimator.predict_proba
390 | 
391 |         Returns
392 |         -------
393 |         C : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_classes)
394 |             The predicted probas.
395 |         """
396 |         check_is_fitted(self)
397 |         # Compute the arithmetic mean of the predictions of the calibrated
398 |         # classifiers
399 |         mean_proba = np.zeros((_num_samples(X), len(self.classes_)))
400 |         for calibrated_classifier in self.calibrated_classifiers_:
401 |             proba = calibrated_classifier.predict_proba(X)
402 |             mean_proba += proba
403 | 
404 |         mean_proba /= len(self.calibrated_classifiers_)
405 | 
406 |         return mean_proba
407 | 
408 |     def predict(self, X):
409 |         """Predict the target of new samples. The predicted class is the
410 |         class that has the highest probability, and can thus be different
411 |         from the prediction of the uncalibrated classifier.
412 | 
413 |         Parameters
414 |         ----------
415 |         X : The samples, as accepted by base_estimator.predict
416 | 
417 |         Returns
418 |         -------
419 |         C : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
420 |             The predicted class.
421 |         """
422 |         check_is_fitted(self)
423 |         return self.classes_[np.argmax(self.predict_proba(X), axis=1)]
424 |

426 |         return {
427 |             "_xfail_checks": {
428 |                 "check_sample_weights_invariance": (
429 |                     "zero sample_weight is not equivalent to removing samples"
430 |                 ),
431 |             }
432 |         }

435 | def _fit_classifier_calibrator_pair(
436 |     estimator, X, y, train, test, supports_sw, method, classes, sample_weight=None
437 | ):
438 |     """Fit a classifier/calibration pair on a given train/test split.
439 | 
440 |     Fit the classifier on the train set, compute its predictions on the test
441 |     set and use the predictions as input to fit the calibrator along with the
442 |     test labels.
443 | 
444 |     Parameters
445 |     ----------
446 |     estimator : estimator instance
447 |         Cloned base estimator.
448 | 
449 |     X : array-like, shape (n_samples, n_features)
450 |         Sample data.
451 | 
452 |     y : array-like, shape (n_samples,)
453 |         Targets.
454 | 
455 |     train : ndarray, shape (n_train_indicies,)
456 |         Indices of the training subset.
457 | 
458 |     test : ndarray, shape (n_test_indicies,)
459 |         Indices of the testing subset.
460 | 
461 |     supports_sw : bool
462 |         Whether or not the `estimator` supports sample weights.
463 | 
464 |     method : {'sigmoid', 'isotonic'}
465 |         Method to use for calibration.
466 | 
467 |     classes : ndarray, shape (n_classes,)
468 |         The target classes.
469 | 
470 |     sample_weight : array-like, default=None
471 |         Sample weights for `X`.
472 | 
473 |     Returns
474 |     -------
475 |     calibrated_classifier : _CalibratedClassifier instance
476 |     """
477 |     X_train, y_train = _safe_indexing(X, train), _safe_indexing(y, train)
478 |     X_test, y_test = _safe_indexing(X, test), _safe_indexing(y, test)
479 |     if supports_sw and sample_weight is not None:
480 |         sw_train = _safe_indexing(sample_weight, train)
481 |         sw_test = _safe_indexing(sample_weight, test)
482 |     else:
483 |         sw_train = None
484 |         sw_test = None
485 | 
486 |     if supports_sw:
487 |         estimator.fit(X_train, y_train, sample_weight=sw_train)
488 |     else:
489 |         estimator.fit(X_train, y_train)
490 | 
491 |     n_classes = len(classes)
492 |     pred_method, method_name = _get_prediction_method(estimator)
493 |     predictions = _compute_predictions(pred_method, method_name, X_test, n_classes)
494 | 
495 |     calibrated_classifier = _fit_calibrator(
496 |         estimator, predictions, y_test, classes, method, sample_weight=sw_test
497 |     )
498 |     return calibrated_classifier
499 |

501 | def _get_prediction_method(clf):
502 |     """Return prediction method.
503 | 
504 |     `decision_function` method of `clf` returned, if it
505 |     exists, otherwise `predict_proba` method returned.
506 | 
507 |     Parameters
508 |     ----------
509 |     clf : Estimator instance
510 |         Fitted classifier to obtain the prediction method from.
511 | 
512 |     Returns
513 |     -------
514 |     prediction_method : callable
515 |         The prediction method.
516 |     method_name : str
517 |         The name of the prediction method.
518 |     """
519 |     if hasattr(clf, "decision_function"):
520 |         method = getattr(clf, "decision_function")
521 |         return method, "decision_function"
522 |     elif hasattr(clf, "predict_proba"):
523 |         method = getattr(clf, "predict_proba")
524 |         return method, "predict_proba"
525 |     else:
526 |         raise RuntimeError(
527 |             "'base_estimator' has no 'decision_function' or 'predict_proba' method."
528 |         )
529 | 
530 | 
531 | def _compute_predictions(pred_method, method_name, X, n_classes):
532 |     """Return predictions for `X` and reshape binary outputs to shape
533 |     (n_samples, 1).
534 | 
535 |     Parameters
536 |     ----------
537 |     pred_method : callable
538 |         Prediction method.
539 | 
540 |     method_name: str
541 |         Name of the prediction method
542 | 
543 |     X : array-like or None
544 |         Data used to obtain predictions.
545 | 
546 |     n_classes : int
547 |         Number of classes present.
548 | 
549 |     Returns
550 |     -------
551 |     predictions : array-like, shape (X.shape[0], len(clf.classes_))
552 |         The predictions. Note if there are 2 classes, array is of shape
553 |         (X.shape[0], 1).
554 |     """
555 |     predictions = pred_method(X=X)
556 | 
557 |     if method_name == "decision_function":
558 |         if predictions.ndim == 1:
559 |             predictions = predictions[:, np.newaxis]
560 |     elif method_name == "predict_proba":
561 |         if n_classes == 2:
562 |             predictions = predictions[:, 1:]
563 |     else:  # pragma: no cover
564 |         # this branch should be unreachable.
565 |         raise ValueError(f"Invalid prediction method: {method_name}")
566 |     return predictions
567 |

569 | def _fit_calibrator(clf, predictions, y, classes, method, sample_weight=None):
570 |     """Fit calibrator(s) and return a `_CalibratedClassifier`
571 |     instance.
572 | 
573 |     `n_classes` (i.e. `len(clf.classes_)`) calibrators are fitted.
574 |     However, if `n_classes` equals 2, one calibrator is fitted.
575 | 
576 |     Parameters
577 |     ----------
578 |     clf : estimator instance
579 |         Fitted classifier.
580 | 
581 |     predictions : array-like, shape (n_samples, n_classes) or (n_samples, 1) \
582 |                     when binary.
583 |         Raw predictions returned by the un-calibrated base classifier.
584 | 
585 |     y : array-like, shape (n_samples,)
586 |         The targets.
587 | 
588 |     classes : ndarray, shape (n_classes,)
589 |         All the prediction classes.
590 | 
591 |     method : {'sigmoid', 'isotonic'}
592 |         The method to use for calibration.
593 | 
594 |     sample_weight : ndarray, shape (n_samples,), default=None
595 |         Sample weights. If None, then samples are equally weighted.
596 | 
597 |     Returns
598 |     -------
599 |     pipeline : _CalibratedClassifier instance
600 |     """
601 |     Y = label_binarize(y, classes=classes)
602 |     label_encoder = LabelEncoder().fit(classes)
603 |     pos_class_indices = label_encoder.transform(clf.classes_)
604 |     calibrators = []
605 |     for class_idx, this_pred in zip(pos_class_indices, predictions.T):
606 |         if method == "isotonic":
607 |             calibrator = IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds="clip")
608 |         elif method == "sigmoid":
609 |             calibrator = _SigmoidCalibration()
610 |         else:
611 |             raise ValueError(
612 |                 f"'method' should be one of: 'sigmoid' or 'isotonic'. Got {method}."
613 |             )
614 |         calibrator.fit(this_pred, Y[:, class_idx], sample_weight)
615 |         calibrators.append(calibrator)
616 | 
617 |     pipeline = _CalibratedClassifier(clf, calibrators, method=method, classes=classes)
618 |     return pipeline

621 | class _CalibratedClassifier:
622 |     """Pipeline-like chaining a fitted classifier and its fitted calibrators.
623 | 
624 |     Parameters
625 |     ----------
626 |     base_estimator : estimator instance
627 |         Fitted classifier.
628 | 
629 |     calibrators : list of fitted estimator instances
630 |         List of fitted calibrators (either 'IsotonicRegression' or
631 |         '_SigmoidCalibration'). The number of calibrators equals the number of
632 |         classes. However, if there are 2 classes, the list contains only one
633 |         fitted calibrator.
634 | 
635 |     classes : array-like of shape (n_classes,)
636 |         All the prediction classes.
637 | 
638 |     method : {'sigmoid', 'isotonic'}, default='sigmoid'
639 |         The method to use for calibration. Can be 'sigmoid' which
640 |         corresponds to Platt's method or 'isotonic' which is a
641 |         non-parametric approach based on isotonic regression.
642 | 
643 |     Attributes
644 |     ----------
645 |     calibrators_ : list of fitted estimator instances
646 |         Same as `calibrators`. Exposed for backward-compatibility. Use
647 |         `calibrators` instead.
648 | 
649 |         .. deprecated:: 0.24
650 |            `calibrators_` is deprecated from 0.24 and will be removed in
651 |            1.1 (renaming of 0.26). Use `calibrators` instead.
652 |     """
653 | 
654 |     def __init__(self, base_estimator, calibrators, *, classes, method="sigmoid"):
655 |         self.base_estimator = base_estimator
656 |         self.calibrators = calibrators
657 |         self.classes = classes
658 |         self.method = method
659 | 
660 |     # TODO: Remove in 1.1
661 |     # mypy error: Decorated property not supported
662 |     @deprecated(  # type: ignore
663 |         "`calibrators_` is deprecated in 0.24 and will be removed in 1.1"
664 |         "(renaming of 0.26). Use `calibrators` instead."
665 |     )
666 |     @property
667 |     def calibrators_(self):
668 |         return self.calibrators
669 | 
670 |     def predict_proba(self, X):
671 |         """Calculate calibrated probabilities.
672 | 
673 |         Calculates classification calibrated probabilities
674 |         for each class, in a one-vs-all manner, for `X`.
675 | 
676 |         Parameters
677 |         ----------
678 |         X : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features)
679 |             The sample data.
680 | 
681 |         Returns
682 |         -------
683 |         proba : array, shape (n_samples, n_classes)
684 |             The predicted probabilities. Can be exact zeros.
685 |         """
686 |         n_classes = len(self.classes)
687 |         pred_method, method_name = _get_prediction_method(self.base_estimator)
688 |         predictions = _compute_predictions(pred_method, method_name, X, n_classes)
689 | 
690 |         label_encoder = LabelEncoder().fit(self.classes)
691 |         pos_class_indices = label_encoder.transform(self.base_estimator.classes_)
692 | 
693 |         proba = np.zeros((_num_samples(X), n_classes))
694 |         for class_idx, this_pred, calibrator in zip(
695 |             pos_class_indices, predictions.T, self.calibrators
696 |         ):
697 |             if n_classes == 2:
698 |                 # When binary, `predictions` consists only of predictions for
699 |                 # clf.classes_[1] but `pos_class_indices` = 0
700 |                 class_idx += 1
701 |             proba[:, class_idx] = calibrator.predict(this_pred)
702 | 
703 |         # Normalize the probabilities
704 |         if n_classes == 2:
705 |             proba[:, 0] = 1.0 - proba[:, 1]
706 |         else:
707 |             denominator = np.sum(proba, axis=1)[:, np.newaxis]
708 |             # In the edge case where for each class calibrator returns a null
709 |             # probability for a given sample, use the uniform distribution
710 |             # instead.
711 |             uniform_proba = np.full_like(proba, 1 / n_classes)
712 |             proba = np.divide(
713 |                 proba, denominator, out=uniform_proba, where=denominator != 0
714 |             )
715 | 
716 |         # Deal with cases where the predicted probability minimally exceeds 1.0
717 |         proba[(1.0 < proba) & (proba <= 1.0 + 1e-5)] = 1.0
718 | 
719 |         return proba
720 |

722 | def _sigmoid_calibration(predictions, y, sample_weight=None):
723 |     """Probability Calibration with sigmoid method (Platt 2000)
724 | 
725 |     Parameters
726 |     ----------
727 |     predictions : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
728 |         The decision function or predict proba for the samples.
729 | 
730 |     y : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
731 |         The targets.
732 | 
733 |     sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
734 |         Sample weights. If None, then samples are equally weighted.
735 | 
736 |     Returns
737 |     -------
738 |     a : float
739 |         The slope.
740 | 
741 |     b : float
742 |         The intercept.
743 | 
744 |     References
745 |     ----------
746 |     Platt, "Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines"
747 |     """
748 |     predictions = column_or_1d(predictions)
749 |     y = column_or_1d(y)
750 | 
751 |     F = predictions  # F follows Platt's notations
752 | 
753 |     # Bayesian priors (see Platt end of section 2.2)
754 |     prior0 = float(np.sum(y <= 0))
755 |     prior1 = y.shape[0] - prior0
756 |     T = np.zeros(y.shape)
757 |     T[y > 0] = (prior1 + 1.0) / (prior1 + 2.0)
758 |     T[y <= 0] = 1.0 / (prior0 + 2.0)
759 |     T1 = 1.0 - T
760 | 
761 |     def objective(AB):
762 |         # From Platt (beginning of Section 2.2)
763 |         P = expit(-(AB[0] * F + AB[1]))
764 |         loss = -(xlogy(T, P) + xlogy(T1, 1.0 - P))
765 |         if sample_weight is not None:
766 |             return (sample_weight * loss).sum()
767 |         else:
768 |             return loss.sum()
769 | 
770 |     def grad(AB):
771 |         # gradient of the objective function
772 |         P = expit(-(AB[0] * F + AB[1]))
773 |         TEP_minus_T1P = T - P
774 |         if sample_weight is not None:
775 |             TEP_minus_T1P *= sample_weight
776 |         dA = np.dot(TEP_minus_T1P, F)
777 |         dB = np.sum(TEP_minus_T1P)
778 |         return np.array([dA, dB])
779 | 
780 |     AB0 = np.array([0.0, log((prior0 + 1.0) / (prior1 + 1.0))])
781 |     AB_ = fmin_bfgs(objective, AB0, fprime=grad, disp=False)
782 |     return AB_[0], AB_[1]
783 | 
784 | 
785 | class _SigmoidCalibration(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
786 |     """Sigmoid regression model.
787 | 
788 |     Attributes
789 |     ----------
790 |     a_ : float
791 |         The slope.
792 | 
793 |     b_ : float
794 |         The intercept.
795 |     """
796 | 
797 |     def fit(self, X, y, sample_weight=None):
798 |         """Fit the model using X, y as training data.
799 | 
800 |         Parameters
801 |         ----------
802 |         X : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
803 |             Training data.
804 | 
805 |         y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
806 |             Training target.
807 | 
808 |         sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
809 |             Sample weights. If None, then samples are equally weighted.
810 | 
811 |         Returns
812 |         -------
813 |         self : object
814 |             Returns an instance of self.
815 |         """
816 |         X = column_or_1d(X)
817 |         y = column_or_1d(y)
818 |         X, y = indexable(X, y)
819 | 
820 |         self.a_, self.b_ = _sigmoid_calibration(X, y, sample_weight)
821 |         return self
822 | 
823 |     def predict(self, T):
824 |         """Predict new data by linear interpolation.
825 | 
826 |         Parameters
827 |         ----------
828 |         T : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
829 |             Data to predict from.
830 | 
831 |         Returns
832 |         -------
833 |         T_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
834 |             The predicted data.
835 |         """
836 |         T = column_or_1d(T)
837 |         return expit(-(self.a_ * T + self.b_))

840 | def calibration_curve(y_true, y_prob, *, normalize=False, n_bins=5, strategy="uniform"):
841 |     """Compute true and predicted probabilities for a calibration curve.
842 | 
843 |     The method assumes the inputs come from a binary classifier, and
844 |     discretize the [0, 1] interval into bins.
845 | 
846 |     Calibration curves may also be referred to as reliability diagrams.
847 | 
848 |     Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <calibration>`.
849 | 
850 |     Parameters
851 |     ----------
852 |     y_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
853 |         True targets.
854 | 
855 |     y_prob : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
856 |         Probabilities of the positive class.
857 | 
858 |     normalize : bool, default=False
859 |         Whether y_prob needs to be normalized into the [0, 1] interval, i.e.
860 |         is not a proper probability. If True, the smallest value in y_prob
861 |         is linearly mapped onto 0 and the largest one onto 1.
862 | 
863 |     n_bins : int, default=5
864 |         Number of bins to discretize the [0, 1] interval. A bigger number
865 |         requires more data. Bins with no samples (i.e. without
866 |         corresponding values in `y_prob`) will not be returned, thus the
867 |         returned arrays may have less than `n_bins` values.
868 | 
869 |     strategy : {'uniform', 'quantile'}, default='uniform'
870 |         Strategy used to define the widths of the bins.
871 | 
872 |         uniform
873 |             The bins have identical widths.
874 |         quantile
875 |             The bins have the same number of samples and depend on `y_prob`.
876 | 
877 |     Returns
878 |     -------
879 |     prob_true : ndarray of shape (n_bins,) or smaller
880 |         The proportion of samples whose class is the positive class, in each
881 |         bin (fraction of positives).
882 | 
883 |     prob_pred : ndarray of shape (n_bins,) or smaller

function.name: explore_tree_structure
function.description:
Unified repository exploring tool that traverses a pre-built code graph to retrieve dependency structure around specified entities.
The search can be controlled to traverse upstream (exploring dependencies that entities rely on) or downstream (exploring how entities impact others), with optional limits on traversal depth and filters for entity and dependency types.

Code Graph Definition:
* Entity Types: 'directory', 'file', 'class', 'function'.
* Dependency Types: 'contains', 'imports', 'invokes', 'inherits'.
* Hierarchy:
    - Directories contain files and subdirectories.
    - Files contain classes and functions.
    - Classes contain inner classes and methods.
    - Functions can contain inner functions.
* Interactions:
    - Files/classes/functions can import classes and functions.
    - Classes can inherit from other classes.
    - Classes and functions can invoke others (invocations in a class's `__init__` are attributed to the class).
Entity ID:
* Unique identifier including file path and module path.
* Here's an example of an Entity ID: `"interface/C.py:C.method_a.inner_func"` identifies function `inner_func` within `method_a` of class `C` in `"interface/C.py"`.

Notes:
* Traversal Control: The `traversal_depth` parameter specifies how deep the function should explore the graph starting from the input entities.
* Filtering: Use `entity_type_filter` and `dependency_type_filter` to narrow down the scope of the search, focusing on specific entity types and relationships.


Example Usage:
1. Exploring Outward Dependencies:
    ```
    explore_tree_structure(
        start_entities=['src/module_a.py:ClassA'],
        direction='downstream',
        traversal_depth=2,
        dependency_type_filter=['invokes', 'imports']
    )
    ```
    This retrieves the dependencies of `ClassA` up to 2 levels deep, focusing only on classes and functions with 'invokes' and 'imports' relationships.

2. Exploring Inward Dependencies:
    ```
    explore_tree_structure(
        start_entities=['src/module_b.py:FunctionY'],
        direction='upstream',
        traversal_depth=-1
    )
    ```
    This finds all entities that depend on `FunctionY` without restricting the traversal depth.
3. Exploring Repository Structure:
    ```
    explore_tree_structure(
      start_entities=['/'],
      traversal_depth=2,
      dependency_type_filter=['contains']
    )
    ```
    This retrieves the tree repository structure from the root directory (/), traversing up to two levels deep and focusing only on 'contains' relationship.
4. Generate Class Diagrams:
    ```
    explore_tree_structure(
        start_entities=selected_entity_ids,
        direction='both',
        traverse_depth=-1,
        dependency_type_filter=['inherits']
    )
    ```

start_entities.description:
List of entities (e.g., class, function, file, or directory paths) to begin the search from.
Entities representing classes or functions must be formatted as "file_path:QualifiedName" (e.g., `interface/C.py:C.method_a.inner_func`).
For files or directories, provide only the file or directory path (e.g., `src/module_a.py` or `src/`).

direction.description:
Direction of traversal in the code graph; allowed options are: `upstream`, `downstream`, `both`.
- 'upstream': Traversal to explore dependencies that the specified entities rely on (how they depend on others).
- 'downstream': Traversal to explore the effects or interactions of the specified entities on others (how others depend on them).
- 'both': Traversal on both direction.

traversal_depth.description: Maximum depth of traversal. A value of -1 indicates unlimited depth (subject to a maximum limit).Must be either `-1` or a non-negative integer (≥ 0).

entity_type_filter.description: List of entity types (e.g., 'class', 'function', 'file', 'directory') to include in the traversal. If None, all entity types are included.

dependency_type_filter.description: List of dependency types (e.g., 'contains', 'imports', 'invokes', 'inherits') to include in the traversal. If None, all dependency types are included.

function.name: get_trace_artifacts
function.description:
Read a compact raw slice of DaLIC execution-trace artifacts for the current instance.
This tool reads '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json' and returns a short JSON summary.
It does not rank or recommend results. It only applies exact filters and pagination.

Note:
'<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json' is generated through a Software Reconnaissance-style analysis, which involves:
- executing two Python scripts describing the same process with (A.py) and without (B.py) the feature enabled.
- tracing their execution, obtain trace A and trace B as the execution traces of A.py and B.py, respectively.
- then subtracting the overlapping parts from trace A and save the rest in '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json'. Therefore it contains the non-overlapping artifacts that only appear in A.py, which are likely to be related to the feature and thus to the issue.

Args:
- `artifact_type`: Optional exact filter for artifact definition type. It can be `function`, `method`, or `class`. 
    If not specified, it defaults to `all` and does not filter by artifact type.
- `path_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to the compact file path. For example, if you are interested in artifacts defined in files under `src/utils`, you can set `path_contains` to `src/utils`. 
    If not specified, it defaults to `None` and does not filter by file path.
- `name_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to the qualified name. For example, if you are interested in artifacts with `DataLoader` in their qualified names, you can set `name_contains` to `DataLoader`. 
    If not specified, it defaults to `None` and does not filter by qualified name.
- `start`: Zero-based pagination offset. It defaults to 0, meaning that the first page starts from the first matched artifact.
- `limit`: Maximum number of artifacts to return in this slice. It defaults to 8, which is a reasonable number for you to inspect at a time. You can adjust it based on your preference and the typical number of matched artifacts.

Returns:
A JSON string encoding an object with the following top-level fields:
- `instance_id`: The current DaLIC instance id.
- `trace_summary`: Summary counts, including `unique_function_count`, `returned_count`, and `filtered_count`.
- `applied_filters`: The effective filter and pagination values used for this call.
- `artifacts`: A JSON array of matched artifacts.
- `has_more`: Whether more matched artifacts are available after this slice.
- `next_start`: The pagination offset to use for the next slice.

Each artifact in `artifacts` is a JSON object with the following fields:
- `qualified_name`: The qualified name of the artifact.
- `path`: The compact file path where the artifact is defined.
- `definition_type`: The raw definition type from DaLIC, such as `function` or `class`.
- `defined_line`: The line number where the artifact is defined.
- `end_line`: The ending line number of the artifact, if available.
- `event_count`: The number of matching execution events in trace A.
- `call_count`: The number of calls observed in trace A.
- `max_call_depth`: The maximum observed call depth for this artifact.

Usage suggestions:
- Call this once near the start of analyzing a new data point to inspect execution-trace evidence.
- Call it again later with narrower `path_contains` or `name_contains` filters whenever you need a more precise slice.

meta_data.problem_statement:
Suggestion: Sliding Window Function
Using `np.lib.stride_tricks.as_stride` one can very efficiently create a sliding window that segments an array as a preprocessing step for vectorized applications. For example a moving average of a window length `3`, stepsize `1`:

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = numpy.lib.stride_tricks.as_strided(
    a, shape=(8, 3), strides=(8, 8)
)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

This is very performant but very hard to do, as the `shape` and `strides` parameters are very hard to understand.

I suggest the implementation of a "simple `sliding_window` function" that does the job of figuring out those two parameters for you.

[The implementation I have been using for years](https://gist.github.com/nils-werner/9d321441006b112a4b116a8387c2280c) allows the above to be replaced by

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = sliding_window(a, size=3, stepsize=1)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

@teoliphant [also has an implementation](https://gist.github.com/teoliphant/96eb779a16bd038e374f2703da62f06d) that would change the above to

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = array_for_sliding_window(a, 3)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

both making it much more readable.

Seeing it is a common usecase in vectorized computing I suggest we put a similar function into NumPy itself.

Regarding to which implementation to follow, they are both assume different things but allow you to do the same thing eventually:

`sliding_window`
- slides over one axis only
- allows setting windowsize and stepsize
- returns array with dimension n+1
- sliding over several axes requires two calls (which come for free as there is no memory reordered)
- has a superfluous `copy` parameter that can be removed and replaced by appending `.copy()` after the call

`array_for_sliding_window`
- slides over all axes simultaneously, window lengths are given as `tuple` parameter
- Assumes a stepsize one in all directions
- returns array with dimension n*2
- stepsize not equal to one requires slicing of output data (unsure if this implies copying data)
- Disabling sliding over `axis[n]` requires you set argument `wshape[n] = 1` or `wshape[n] = a.shape[n]`

This means for flexible `stepsize` the following are equivalent (with some minor bug in `sliding_window` there):

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
print sliding_window(a, size=3, stepsize=2)

a = numpy.arange(10)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, 3)[::2, :] # Stepsize 2 by dropping every 2nd row
```

for sliding over one `axis` the following are equivalent (with some transposing and squeezing):

```
a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print sliding_window(a, size=3, axis=1)

a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, (1, 3))
```

and for sliding over two `axis` the following are equivalent:

```
a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print sliding_window(sliding_window(a, size=3, axis=0), size=2, axis=1)

a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, (3, 2))
```

This issue is about sparking discussion about
- Do we need such a function?
- Which features are required?
- Which interface should we persue?

After discussion I am willing to draft up a pull request with an implementation we agreed on.

+        ``x_shape_trimmed`` is ``x.shape`` with every entry reduced by one less

+    Notes

+    For many applications using a sliding window view can be convenient, but
+    potentially very slow. Often specialized solutions exist, for example:
+
+    - `scipy.signal.fftconvolve`
+
+    - filtering functions in `scipy.ndimage`
+

+    algorithm can achieve `O(N)`. That means that the sliding window variant
+    for a window size of 100 can be a 100 times slower than a more specialized

+            [[ 2,  3],
+             [12, 13]]],

+            [[11, 12],

+    (3, 1, 2, 3)
+    >>> v
+    array([[[[ 0,  1,  2],
+             [ 1,  2,  3]]],
+           [[[10, 11, 12],
+             [11, 12, 13]]],

+    views which skip elements:

+    >>> v.shape

search_code_snippets(search_terms: Optional[List[str]] = None, line_nums: Optional[List] = None, file_path_or_pattern: Optional[str] = '**/*.py') -> str:
    Searches the codebase to retrieve relevant code snippets based on given queries(terms or line numbers).
    This function supports retrieving the complete content of a code entity,
    searching for code entities such as classes or functions by keywords, or locating specific lines within a file.
    It also supports filtering searches based on a file path or file pattern.
    Note:
    1. If `search_terms` are provided, it searches for code snippets based on each term:
    - If a term is formatted as 'file_path:QualifiedName' (e.g., 'src/helpers/math_helpers.py:MathUtils.calculate_sum') ,
    or just 'file_path', the corresponding complete code is retrieved or file content is retrieved.
    - If a term matches a file, class, or function name, matched entities are retrieved.
    - If there is no match with any module name, it attempts to find code snippets that likely contain the term.
    2. If `line_nums` is provided, it searches for code snippets at the specified lines within the file defined by
    `file_path_or_pattern`.
    Args:
    search_terms (Optional[List[str]]): A list of names, keywords, or code snippets to search for within the codebase.
    Terms can be formatted as 'file_path:QualifiedName' to search for a specific module or entity within a file
    (e.g., 'src/helpers/math_helpers.py:MathUtils.calculate_sum') or as 'file_path' to retrieve the complete content
    of a file. This can also include potential function names, class names, or general code fragments.
    line_nums (Optional[List[int]]): Specific line numbers to locate code snippets within a specified file.
    When provided, `file_path_or_pattern` must specify a valid file path.
    file_path_or_pattern (Optional[str]): A glob pattern or specific file path used to filter search results
    to particular files or directories. Defaults to '**/*.py', meaning all Python files are searched by default.
    If `line_nums` are provided, this must specify a specific file path.
    Returns:
    str: The search results, which may include code snippets, matching entities, or complete file content.
    Example Usage:
    # Search for the full content of a specific file
    result = search_code_snippets(search_terms=['src/my_file.py'])
    # Search for a specific function
    result = search_code_snippets(search_terms=['src/my_file.py:MyClass.func_name'])
    # Search for specific lines (10 and 15) within a file
    result = search_code_snippets(line_nums=[10, 15], file_path_or_pattern='src/example.py')
    # Combined search for a module name and within a specific file pattern
    result = search_code_snippets(search_terms=["MyClass"], file_path_or_pattern="src/**/*.py")

explore_tree_structure(start_entities: List[str], direction: str = 'downstream', traversal_depth: int = 2, entity_type_filter: Optional[List[str]] = None, dependency_type_filter: Optional[List[str]] = None):
    Analyzes and displays the dependency structure around specified entities in a code graph.
    This function searches and presents relationships and dependencies for the specified entities (such as classes, functions, files, or directories) in a code graph.
    It explores how the input entities relate to others, using defined types of dependencies, including 'contains', 'imports', 'invokes' and 'inherits'.
    The search can be controlled to traverse upstream (exploring dependencies that entities rely on) or downstream (exploring how entities impact others), with optional limits on traversal depth and filters for entity and dependency types.
    Example Usage:
    1. Exploring Outward Dependencies:
    ```
    get_local_structure(
    start_entities=['src/module_a.py:ClassA'],
    direction='downstream',
    traversal_depth=2,
    entity_type_filter=['class', 'function'],
    dependency_type_filter=['invokes', 'imports']
    )
    ```
    This retrieves the dependencies of `ClassA` up to 2 levels deep, focusing only on classes and functions with 'invokes' and 'imports' relationships.
    2. Exploring Inward Dependencies:
    ```
    get_local_structure(
    start_entities=['src/module_b.py:FunctionY'],
    direction='upstream',
    traversal_depth=-1
    )
    ```
    This finds all entities that depend on `FunctionY` without restricting the traversal depth.
    Notes:
    * Traversal Control: The `traversal_depth` parameter specifies how deep the function should explore the graph starting from the input entities.
    * Filtering: Use `entity_type_filter` and `dependency_type_filter` to narrow down the scope of the search, focusing on specific entity types and relationships.
    * Graph Context: The function operates on a pre-built code graph containing entities (e.g., files, classes and functions) and dependencies representing their interactions and relationships.
    Parameters:
    ----------
    start_entities : list[str]
    List of entities (e.g., class, function, file, or directory paths) to begin the search from.
    - Entities representing classes or functions must be formatted as "file_path:QualifiedName"
    (e.g., `interface/C.py:C.method_a.inner_func`).
    - For files or directories, provide only the file or directory path (e.g., `src/module_a.py` or `src/`).
    direction : str, optional
    Direction of traversal in the code graph; allowed options are:
    - 'upstream': Traversal to explore dependencies that the specified entities rely on (how they depend on others).
    - 'downstream': Traversal to explore the effects or interactions of the specified entities on others
    (how others depend on them).
    - 'both': Traversal in both directions.
    Default is 'downstream'.
    traversal_depth : int, optional
    Maximum depth of traversal. A value of -1 indicates unlimited depth (subject to a maximum limit).
    Must be either `-1` or a non-negative integer (≥ 0).
    Default is 2.
    entity_type_filter : list[str], optional
    List of entity types (e.g., 'class', 'function', 'file', 'directory') to include in the traversal.
    If None, all entity types are included.
    Default is None.
    dependency_type_filter : list[str], optional
    List of dependency types (e.g., 'contains', 'imports', 'invokes', 'inherits') to include in the traversal.
    If None, all dependency types are included.
    Default is None.
    Returns:
    -------
    result : object
    An object representing the traversal results, which includes discovered entities and their dependencies.

get_trace_artifacts(artifact_type: str = 'all', path_contains: str | None = None, name_contains: str | None = None, start: int = 0, limit: int = 8):
    Read a compact raw slice of DaLIC execution-trace artifacts for the current instance.
    This tool reads '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json' and returns a short JSON summary.
    It does not rank or recommend results. It only applies filters and pagination.
    Note:
    '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json' is generated through a Software Reconnaissance-style analysis, which involves:
    - executing two Python scripts describing the same process with (A.py) and without (B.py) the feature enabled.
    - tracing their execution, obtain trace A and trace B as the execution traces of A.py and B.py, respectively.
    - then subtracting the overlapping parts from trace A and save the rest in '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json'. Therefore it contains the non-overlapping artifacts that only appear in A.py, which are likely to be related to the feature and thus to the issue.
    Args:
    - `artifact_type`: Optional exact filter for artifact definition type. It can be `function`, `method`, or `class`.
    If not specified, it defaults to `all` and does not filter by artifact type.
    - `path_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to the compact file path. For example, if you are interested in artifacts defined in files under `src/utils`, you can set `path_contains` to `src/utils`.
    If not specified, it defaults to `None` and does not filter by file path.
    - `name_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to the qualified name. For example, if you are interested in artifacts with `DataLoader` in their qualified names, you can set `name_contains` to `DataLoader`.
    If not specified, it defaults to `None` and does not filter by qualified name.
    - `start`: Zero-based pagination offset. It defaults to 0, meaning that the first page starts from the first matched artifact.
    - `limit`: Maximum number of artifacts to return in this slice. It defaults to 8, which is a reasonable number for you to inspect at a time. You can adjust it based on your preference and the typical number of matched artifacts.
    Returns:
    A JSON string encoding an object with the following top-level fields:
    - `instance_id`: The current DaLIC instance id.
    - `trace_summary`: Summary counts, including `unique_function_count`, `returned_count`, and `filtered_count`.
    - `applied_filters`: The effective filter and pagination values used for this call.
    - `artifacts`: A JSON array of matched artifacts.
    - `has_more`: Whether more matched artifacts are available after this slice.
    - `next_start`: The pagination offset to use for the next slice.
    Each artifact in `artifacts` is a JSON object with the following fields:
    - `qualified_name`: The qualified name of the artifact.
    - `path`: The compact file path where the artifact is defined.
    - `definition_type`: The raw definition type from DaLIC, such as `function` or `class`.
    - `defined_line`: The line number where the artifact is defined.
    - `end_line`: The ending line number of the artifact, if available.
    - `event_count`: The number of matching execution events in trace A.
    - `call_count`: The number of calls observed in trace A.
    - `max_call_depth`: The maximum observed call depth for this artifact.
    Usage suggestions:
    - Call this once near the start of analyzing a new data point to inspect execution-trace evidence.
    - Call it again later with narrower `path_contains` or `name_contains` filters whenever you need a more precise slice.

get_trace_data_dependencies(symbol_contains: str | None = None, scope_contains: str | None = None, path_contains: str | None = None, edge_type: str | None = None, start: int = 0, limit: int = 12, path_limit: int = 4):
    Read a compact raw slice of DaLIC data-dependency evidence for the current instance.
    This tool reads '<instance_id>/unique_dep_tree.json' and returns a short JSON summary.
    It does not rank or recommend results. It only applies filters and pagination.
    Note:
    - '<instance_id>/unique_dep_tree.json' is generated by analyzing the data dependencies of the unique artifacts in '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json'.
    - It contains the dataflows associated with the unique artifacts, which can help you understand how the unique artifacts are related to each other and how they are related to other parts of the codebase.
    Args:
    - `symbol_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to symbol names.
    For example, if you are interested in dependencies related to symbols with `DataLoader` in their names, you can set `symbol_contains` to `DataLoader`.
    Together with `scope_contains` and `path_contains`, this first selects a set of matching symbols; an edge is retained when either endpoint belongs to that set.
    If not specified, it defaults to `None`
    - `scope_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to symbol scopes.
    The scope is represented as a dot-separated string of nested scopes, such as `src.utils.data_loader.DataLoader.__init__`.
    You can set `scope_contains` to a substring of the scope to filter dependencies related to that scope.
    For example, setting it to `DataLoader` would match the above scope and include its dependencies.
    Together with `symbol_contains` and `path_contains`, this contributes to the symbol-matching step described above.
    If not specified, it defaults to `None`
    - `path_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to compact file paths.
    For example, if you are interested in dependencies related to files under `src/utils`, you can set `path_contains` to `src/utils`.
    Together with `symbol_contains` and `scope_contains`, this contributes to the symbol-matching step described above.
    If not specified, it defaults to `None`
    - `edge_type`: Optional exact filter for dependency edge type such as `data` or `ret`. If not specified, it defaults to `None` and does not filter by edge type.
    - `start`: Zero-based pagination offset for matched edges. It defaults to 0, meaning that the first page starts from the first matched edge.
    - `limit`: Maximum number of matched edges to return in this slice. It defaults to 12, which is a reasonable number for you to inspect at a time.
    You can adjust it based on your preference and the typical number of matched edges.
    - `path_limit`: Maximum number of compact dependency paths to include. A dependency path is a sequence of dependency edges connecting two symbols.
    If there are more matched paths than this limit, only the first few unique compressed paths are returned.
    Important behavior:
    - If at least one symbol matches the combined `symbol_contains` / `scope_contains` / `path_contains` filters, only edges whose source or destination is in that matched symbol set are retained.
    - If no symbol matches those filters, edge filtering falls back to `edge_type` plus pagination only; it does not return an empty edge list.
    Returns:
    A JSON string encoding an object with the following top-level fields:
    - `instance_id`: The current DaLIC instance id.
    - `dep_summary`: Summary counts, including retained file / symbol / edge counts and the returned / filtered edge counts.
    - `applied_filters`: The effective filter and pagination values used for this call.
    - `matched_symbols`: A compact JSON array of symbols related to the current page of results.
    - `edges`: A JSON array of matched dependency edges.
    - `paths`: A JSON array of compressed dependency-path strings related to the current page.
    - `has_more`: Whether more matched edges are available after this slice.
    - `next_start`: The pagination offset to use for the next slice.
    Each symbol in `matched_symbols` has these fields:
    - `kind`: The raw symbol kind from DaLIC, such as `func`, `class`, or similar labels.
    - `symbol`: The symbol name.
    - `scope`: The raw scope string associated with the symbol.
    - `path`: The compact file path where the symbol is defined.
    - `line`: The line number where the symbol is defined.
    Each edge in `edges` is a JSON object with the following fields:
    - `src`: A compact source-symbol object with fields `kind`, `symbol`, `scope`, `path`, and `line`.
    - `dst`: A compact target-symbol object with fields `kind`, `symbol`, `scope`, `path`, and `line`.
    - `edge_type`: The raw dependency edge type, such as `arg`, `data`, or `ret`.
    Usage suggestions:
    - Use it whenever you need a focused dependency slice around a traced symbol, scope, or file path.
    - During analysis, you may call it again with narrower `symbol_contains`, `scope_contains`, `path_contains`, or `edge_type` filters.

---- BEGIN FUNCTION #4: explore_tree_structure ----
Description: 
Unified repository exploring tool that traverses a pre-built code graph to retrieve dependency structure around specified entities.
The search can be controlled to traverse upstream (exploring dependencies that entities rely on) or downstream (exploring how entities impact others), with optional limits on traversal depth and filters for entity and dependency types.

Code Graph Definition:
* Entity Types: 'directory', 'file', 'class', 'function'.
* Dependency Types: 'contains', 'imports', 'invokes', 'inherits'.
* Hierarchy:
    - Directories contain files and subdirectories.
    - Files contain classes and functions.
    - Classes contain inner classes and methods.
    - Functions can contain inner functions.
* Interactions:
    - Files/classes/functions can import classes and functions.
    - Classes can inherit from other classes.
    - Classes and functions can invoke others (invocations in a class's `__init__` are attributed to the class).
Entity ID:
* Unique identifier including file path and module path.
* Here's an example of an Entity ID: `"interface/C.py:C.method_a.inner_func"` identifies function `inner_func` within `method_a` of class `C` in `"interface/C.py"`.

Notes:
* Traversal Control: The `traversal_depth` parameter specifies how deep the function should explore the graph starting from the input entities.
* Filtering: Use `entity_type_filter` and `dependency_type_filter` to narrow down the scope of the search, focusing on specific entity types and relationships.


Example Usage:
1. Exploring Outward Dependencies:
    ```
    explore_tree_structure(
        start_entities=['src/module_a.py:ClassA'],
        direction='downstream',
        traversal_depth=2,
        dependency_type_filter=['invokes', 'imports']
    )
    ```
    This retrieves the dependencies of `ClassA` up to 2 levels deep, focusing only on classes and functions with 'invokes' and 'imports' relationships.

2. Exploring Inward Dependencies:
    ```
    explore_tree_structure(
        start_entities=['src/module_b.py:FunctionY'],
        direction='upstream',
        traversal_depth=-1
    )
    ```
    This finds all entities that depend on `FunctionY` without restricting the traversal depth.
3. Exploring Repository Structure:
    ```
    explore_tree_structure(
      start_entities=['/'],
      traversal_depth=2,
      dependency_type_filter=['contains']
    )
    ```
    This retrieves the tree repository structure from the root directory (/), traversing up to two levels deep and focusing only on 'contains' relationship.
4. Generate Class Diagrams:
    ```
    explore_tree_structure(
        start_entities=selected_entity_ids,
        direction='both',
        traverse_depth=-1,
        dependency_type_filter=['inherits']
    )
    ```

Parameters:
  (1) start_entities (array, required): List of entities (e.g., class, function, file, or directory paths) to begin the search from.
Entities representing classes or functions must be formatted as "file_path:QualifiedName" (e.g., `interface/C.py:C.method_a.inner_func`).
For files or directories, provide only the file or directory path (e.g., `src/module_a.py` or `src/`).
  (2) direction (string, optional): Direction of traversal in the code graph; allowed options are: `upstream`, `downstream`, `both`.
- 'upstream': Traversal to explore dependencies that the specified entities rely on (how they depend on others).
- 'downstream': Traversal to explore the effects or interactions of the specified entities on others (how others depend on them).
- 'both': Traversal on both direction.
Allowed values: [`upstream`, `downstream`, `both`]
  (3) traversal_depth (integer, optional): Maximum depth of traversal. A value of -1 indicates unlimited depth (subject to a maximum limit).Must be either `-1` or a non-negative integer (≥ 0).
  (4) entity_type_filter (['array', 'null'], optional): List of entity types (e.g., 'class', 'function', 'file', 'directory') to include in the traversal. If None, all entity types are included.
  (5) dependency_type_filter (['array', 'null'], optional): List of dependency types (e.g., 'contains', 'imports', 'invokes', 'inherits') to include in the traversal. If None, all dependency types are included.
---- END FUNCTION #4 ----

Description: 
Read a compact raw slice of DaLIC execution-trace artifacts for the current instance.
This tool reads '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json' and returns a short JSON summary.
It does not rank or recommend results. It only applies exact filters and pagination.

Note:
'<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json' is generated through a Software Reconnaissance-style analysis, which involves:
- executing two Python scripts describing the same process with (A.py) and without (B.py) the feature enabled.
- tracing their execution, obtain trace A and trace B as the execution traces of A.py and B.py, respectively.
- then subtracting the overlapping parts from trace A and save the rest in '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json'. Therefore it contains the non-overlapping artifacts that only appear in A.py, which are likely to be related to the feature and thus to the issue.

Args:
- `artifact_type`: Optional exact filter for artifact definition type. It can be `function`, `method`, or `class`. 
    If not specified, it defaults to `all` and does not filter by artifact type.
- `path_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to the compact file path. For example, if you are interested in artifacts defined in files under `src/utils`, you can set `path_contains` to `src/utils`. 
    If not specified, it defaults to `None` and does not filter by file path.
- `name_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to the qualified name. For example, if you are interested in artifacts with `DataLoader` in their qualified names, you can set `name_contains` to `DataLoader`. 
    If not specified, it defaults to `None` and does not filter by qualified name.
- `start`: Zero-based pagination offset. It defaults to 0, meaning that the first page starts from the first matched artifact.
- `limit`: Maximum number of artifacts to return in this slice. It defaults to 8, which is a reasonable number for you to inspect at a time. You can adjust it based on your preference and the typical number of matched artifacts.

Returns:
A JSON string encoding an object with the following top-level fields:
- `instance_id`: The current DaLIC instance id.
- `trace_summary`: Summary counts, including `unique_function_count`, `returned_count`, and `filtered_count`.
- `applied_filters`: The effective filter and pagination values used for this call.
- `artifacts`: A JSON array of matched artifacts.
- `has_more`: Whether more matched artifacts are available after this slice.
- `next_start`: The pagination offset to use for the next slice.

Each artifact in `artifacts` is a JSON object with the following fields:
- `qualified_name`: The qualified name of the artifact.
- `path`: The compact file path where the artifact is defined.
- `definition_type`: The raw definition type from DaLIC, such as `function` or `class`.
- `defined_line`: The line number where the artifact is defined.
- `end_line`: The ending line number of the artifact, if available.
- `event_count`: The number of matching execution events in trace A.
- `call_count`: The number of calls observed in trace A.
- `max_call_depth`: The maximum observed call depth for this artifact.

Usage suggestions:
- Call this once near the start of analyzing a new data point to inspect execution-trace evidence.
- Call it again later with narrower `path_contains` or `name_contains` filters whenever you need a more precise slice.

Parameters:
  (1) artifact_type (string, optional): Optional exact filter for artifact definition type.
Allowed values: [`all`, `function`, `method`, `class`]
  (2) path_contains (['string', 'null'], optional): Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to the compact file path.
  (3) name_contains (['string', 'null'], optional): Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to the qualified name.
  (4) start (integer, optional): Zero-based pagination offset.
  (5) limit (integer, optional): Maximum number of artifacts to return in this slice.
---- END FUNCTION #5 ----

Description: 
Read a compact raw slice of DaLIC data-dependency evidence for the current instance.
This tool reads '<instance_id>/unique_dep_tree.json' and returns a short JSON summary.
It does not rank or recommend results. It only applies filters and pagination.

Note:
- '<instance_id>/unique_dep_tree.json' is generated by analyzing the data dependencies of the unique artifacts in '<instance_id>/unique_artifacts.json'.  
- It contains the dataflows associated with the unique artifacts, which can help you understand how the unique artifacts are related to each other and how they are related to other parts of the codebase.

Args:
- `symbol_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to symbol names. 
    For example, if you are interested in dependencies related to symbols with `DataLoader` in their names, you can set `symbol_contains` to `DataLoader`. 
    Together with `scope_contains` and `path_contains`, this first selects a set of matching symbols; an edge is retained when either endpoint belongs to that set.
    If not specified, it defaults to `None`
- `scope_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to symbol scopes. 
    The scope is represented as a dot-separated string of nested scopes, such as `src.utils.data_loader.DataLoader.__init__`. 
    You can set `scope_contains` to a substring of the scope to filter dependencies related to that scope. 
    For example, setting it to `DataLoader` would match the above scope and include its dependencies.
    Together with `symbol_contains` and `path_contains`, this contributes to the symbol-matching step described above.
    If not specified, it defaults to `None`
- `path_contains`: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to compact file paths.
    For example, if you are interested in dependencies related to files under `src/utils`, you can set `path_contains` to `src/utils`. 
    Together with `symbol_contains` and `scope_contains`, this contributes to the symbol-matching step described above.
    If not specified, it defaults to `None`
- `edge_type`: Optional exact filter for dependency edge type such as `data` or `ret`. If not specified, it defaults to `None` and does not filter by edge type.
- `start`: Zero-based pagination offset for matched edges. It defaults to 0, meaning that the first page starts from the first matched edge.
- `limit`: Maximum number of matched edges to return in this slice. It defaults to 12, which is a reasonable number for you to inspect at a time. 
    You can adjust it based on your preference and the typical number of matched edges.
- `path_limit`: Maximum number of compact dependency paths to include. A dependency path is a sequence of dependency edges connecting two symbols. 
    If there are more matched paths than this limit, only the first few unique compressed paths are returned.

Important behavior:
- If at least one symbol matches the combined `symbol_contains` / `scope_contains` / `path_contains` filters, only edges whose source or destination is in that matched symbol set are retained.
- If no symbol matches those filters, edge filtering falls back to `edge_type` plus pagination only; it does not return an empty edge list.

Returns:
A JSON string encoding an object with the following top-level fields:
- `instance_id`: The current DaLIC instance id.
- `dep_summary`: Summary counts, including retained file / symbol / edge counts and the returned / filtered edge counts.
- `applied_filters`: The effective filter and pagination values used for this call.
- `matched_symbols`: A compact JSON array of symbols related to the current page of results.
- `edges`: A JSON array of matched dependency edges.
- `paths`: A JSON array of compressed dependency-path strings related to the current page.
- `has_more`: Whether more matched edges are available after this slice.
- `next_start`: The pagination offset to use for the next slice.

Each symbol in `matched_symbols` has these fields:
- `kind`: The raw symbol kind from DaLIC, such as `func`, `class`, or similar labels.
- `symbol`: The symbol name.
- `scope`: The raw scope string associated with the symbol.
- `path`: The compact file path where the symbol is defined.
- `line`: The line number where the symbol is defined.

Each edge in `edges` is a JSON object with the following fields:
- `src`: A compact source-symbol object with fields `kind`, `symbol`, `scope`, `path`, and `line`.
- `dst`: A compact target-symbol object with fields `kind`, `symbol`, `scope`, `path`, and `line`.
- `edge_type`: The raw dependency edge type, such as `arg`, `data`, or `ret`.

Usage suggestions:
- Use it whenever you need a focused dependency slice around a traced symbol, scope, or file path.
- During analysis, you may call it again with narrower `symbol_contains`, `scope_contains`, `path_contains`, or `edge_type` filters.

Parameters:
  (1) symbol_contains (['string', 'null'], optional): Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to symbol names.
  (2) scope_contains (['string', 'null'], optional): Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to symbol scopes.
  (3) path_contains (['string', 'null'], optional): Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to compact file paths.
  (4) edge_type (['string', 'null'], optional): Optional exact filter for dependency edge type such as `data` or `ret`.
  (5) start (integer, optional): Zero-based pagination offset for matched edges.
  (6) limit (integer, optional): Maximum number of matched edges to return in this slice.
  (7) path_limit (integer, optional): Maximum number of compact dependency paths to include.

Title: Suggestion: Sliding Window Function

Using `np.lib.stride_tricks.as_stride` one can very efficiently create a sliding window that segments an array as a preprocessing step for vectorized applications. For example a moving average of a window length `3`, stepsize `1`:

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = numpy.lib.stride_tricks.as_strided(
    a, shape=(8, 3), strides=(8, 8)
)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

This is very performant but very hard to do, as the `shape` and `strides` parameters are very hard to understand.

I suggest the implementation of a "simple `sliding_window` function" that does the job of figuring out those two parameters for you.

[The implementation I have been using for years](https://gist.github.com/nils-werner/9d321441006b112a4b116a8387c2280c) allows the above to be replaced by

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = sliding_window(a, size=3, stepsize=1)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

@teoliphant [also has an implementation](https://gist.github.com/teoliphant/96eb779a16bd038e374f2703da62f06d) that would change the above to

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = array_for_sliding_window(a, 3)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

both making it much more readable.

Seeing it is a common usecase in vectorized computing I suggest we put a similar function into NumPy itself.

Regarding to which implementation to follow, they are both assume different things but allow you to do the same thing eventually:

`sliding_window`
- slides over one axis only
- allows setting windowsize and stepsize
- returns array with dimension n+1
- sliding over several axes requires two calls (which come for free as there is no memory reordered)
- has a superfluous `copy` parameter that can be removed and replaced by appending `.copy()` after the call

`array_for_sliding_window`
- slides over all axes simultaneously, window lengths are given as `tuple` parameter
- Assumes a stepsize one in all directions
- returns array with dimension n*2
- stepsize not equal to one requires slicing of output data (unsure if this implies copying data)
- Disabling sliding over `axis[n]` requires you set argument `wshape[n] = 1` or `wshape[n] = a.shape[n]`

This means for flexible `stepsize` the following are equivalent (with some minor bug in `sliding_window` there):

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
print sliding_window(a, size=3, stepsize=2)

a = numpy.arange(10)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, 3)[::2, :] # Stepsize 2 by dropping every 2nd row
```

for sliding over one `axis` the following are equivalent (with some transposing and squeezing):

```
a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print sliding_window(a, size=3, axis=1)

a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, (1, 3))
```

and for sliding over two `axis` the following are equivalent:

```
a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print sliding_window(sliding_window(a, size=3, axis=0), size=2, axis=1)

a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, (3, 2))
```

This issue is about sparking discussion about
- Do we need such a function?
- Which features are required?
- Which interface should we persue?

After discussion I am willing to draft up a pull request with an implementation we agreed on.
--- END PROBLEM STATEMENT ---

 502 |

 519 |     Examples
 520 |     --------
 521 | 
 522 |     np.array allows to specify whether the array is written in C-contiguous
 523 |     order (last index varies the fastest), or FORTRAN-contiguous order in
 524 |     memory (first index varies the fastest).
 525 | 
 526 |     >>> a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], order='C')
 527 |     >>> a
 528 |     array([[1, 2, 3],
 529 |            [4, 5, 6]])
 530 |     >>> np.isfortran(a)
 531 |     False
 532 | 
 533 |     >>> b = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], order='F')
 534 |     >>> b
 535 |     array([[1, 2, 3],
 536 |            [4, 5, 6]])
 537 |     >>> np.isfortran(b)
 538 |     True
 539 | 
 540 | 
 541 |     The transpose of a C-ordered array is a FORTRAN-ordered array.
 542 | 
 543 |     >>> a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], order='C')
 544 |     >>> a
 545 |     array([[1, 2, 3],
 546 |            [4, 5, 6]])
 547 |     >>> np.isfortran(a)
 548 |     False
 549 |     >>> b = a.T
 550 |     >>> b
 551 |     array([[1, 4],
 552 |            [2, 5],
 553 |            [3, 6]])
 554 |     >>> np.isfortran(b)
 555 |     True
 556 | 
 557 |     C-ordered arrays evaluate as False even if they are also FORTRAN-ordered.
 558 | 
 559 |     >>> np.isfortran(np.array([1, 2], order='F'))
 560 |     False
 561 | 
 562 |     """
 563 |     return a.flags.fnc

 680 | @array_function_dispatch(_correlate_dispatcher)
 681 | def correlate(a, v, mode='valid'):
 682 |     """
 683 |     Cross-correlation of two 1-dimensional sequences.
 684 | 
 685 |     This function computes the correlation as generally defined in signal
 686 |     processing texts::
 687 | 
 688 |         c_{av}[k] = sum_n a[n+k] * conj(v[n])
 689 | 
 690 |     with a and v sequences being zero-padded where necessary and conj being
 691 |     the conjugate.
 692 | 
 693 |     Parameters
 694 |     ----------
 695 |     a, v : array_like
 696 |         Input sequences.
 697 |     mode : {'valid', 'same', 'full'}, optional
 698 |         Refer to the `convolve` docstring.  Note that the default
 699 |         is 'valid', unlike `convolve`, which uses 'full'.
 700 |     old_behavior : bool
 701 |         `old_behavior` was removed in NumPy 1.10. If you need the old
 702 |         behavior, use `multiarray.correlate`.
 703 | 
 704 |     Returns
 705 |     -------
 706 |     out : ndarray
 707 |         Discrete cross-correlation of `a` and `v`.
 708 | 
 709 |     See Also
 710 |     --------
 711 |     convolve : Discrete, linear convolution of two one-dimensional sequences.
 712 |     multiarray.correlate : Old, no conjugate, version of correlate.
 713 | 
 714 |     Notes
 715 |     -----
 716 |     The definition of correlation above is not unique and sometimes correlation
 717 |     may be defined differently. Another common definition is::
 718 | 
 719 |         c'_{av}[k] = sum_n a[n] conj(v[n+k])
 720 | 
 721 |     which is related to ``c_{av}[k]`` by ``c'_{av}[k] = c_{av}[-k]``.
 722 | 
 723 |     Examples
 724 |     --------
 725 |     >>> np.correlate([1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 0.5])
 726 |     array([3.5])
 727 |     >>> np.correlate([1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 0.5], "same")
 728 |     array([2. ,  3.5,  3. ])
 729 |     >>> np.correlate([1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 0.5], "full")
 730 |     array([0.5,  2. ,  3.5,  3. ,  0. ])
 731 | 
 732 |     Using complex sequences:
 733 | 
 734 |     >>> np.correlate([1+1j, 2, 3-1j], [0, 1, 0.5j], 'full')
 735 |     array([ 0.5-0.5j,  1.0+0.j ,  1.5-1.5j,  3.0-1.j ,  0.0+0.j ])
 736 | 
 737 |     Note that you get the time reversed, complex conjugated result
 738 |     when the two input sequences change places, i.e.,
 739 |     ``c_{va}[k] = c^{*}_{av}[-k]``:
 740 | 
 741 |     >>> np.correlate([0, 1, 0.5j], [1+1j, 2, 3-1j], 'full')
 742 |     array([ 0.0+0.j ,  3.0+1.j ,  1.5+1.5j,  1.0+0.j ,  0.5+0.5j])
 743 | 
 744 |     """
 745 |     mode = _mode_from_name(mode)
 746 |     return multiarray.correlate2(a, v, mode)
 747 |

 753 | @array_function_dispatch(_convolve_dispatcher)
 754 | def convolve(a, v, mode='full'):
 755 |     """
 756 |     Returns the discrete, linear convolution of two one-dimensional sequences.
 757 | 
 758 |     The convolution operator is often seen in signal processing, where it
 759 |     models the effect of a linear time-invariant system on a signal [1]_.  In
 760 |     probability theory, the sum of two independent random variables is
 761 |     distributed according to the convolution of their individual
 762 |     distributions.
 763 | 
 764 |     If `v` is longer than `a`, the arrays are swapped before computation.
 765 | 
 766 |     Parameters
 767 |     ----------
 768 |     a : (N,) array_like
 769 |         First one-dimensional input array.
 770 |     v : (M,) array_like
 771 |         Second one-dimensional input array.
 772 |     mode : {'full', 'valid', 'same'}, optional
 773 |         'full':
 774 |           By default, mode is 'full'.  This returns the convolution
 775 |           at each point of overlap, with an output shape of (N+M-1,). At
 776 |           the end-points of the convolution, the signals do not overlap
 777 |           completely, and boundary effects may be seen.
 778 | 
 779 |         'same':
 780 |           Mode 'same' returns output of length ``max(M, N)``.  Boundary
 781 |           effects are still visible.
 782 | 
 783 |         'valid':
 784 |           Mode 'valid' returns output of length
 785 |           ``max(M, N) - min(M, N) + 1``.  The convolution product is only given
 786 |           for points where the signals overlap completely.  Values outside
 787 |           the signal boundary have no effect.
 788 | 
 789 |     Returns
 790 |     -------
 791 |     out : ndarray
 792 |         Discrete, linear convolution of `a` and `v`.
 793 | 
 794 |     See Also
 795 |     --------
 796 |     scipy.signal.fftconvolve : Convolve two arrays using the Fast Fourier
 797 |                                Transform.
 798 |     scipy.linalg.toeplitz : Used to construct the convolution operator.
 799 |     polymul : Polynomial multiplication. Same output as convolve, but also
 800 |               accepts poly1d objects as input.
 801 | 
 802 |     Notes
 803 |     -----
 804 |     The discrete convolution operation is defined as
 805 | 
 806 |     .. math:: (a * v)[n] = \\sum_{m = -\\infty}^{\\infty} a[m] v[n - m]
 807 | 
 808 |     It can be shown that a convolution :math:`x(t) * y(t)` in time/space
 809 |     is equivalent to the multiplication :math:`X(f) Y(f)` in the Fourier
 810 |     domain, after appropriate padding (padding is necessary to prevent
 811 |     circular convolution).  Since multiplication is more efficient (faster)
 812 |     than convolution, the function `scipy.signal.fftconvolve` exploits the
 813 |     FFT to calculate the convolution of large data-sets.
 814 | 
 815 |     References
 816 |     ----------
 817 |     .. [1] Wikipedia, "Convolution",
 818 |         https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution
 819 | 
 820 |     Examples
 821 |     --------
 822 |     Note how the convolution operator flips the second array
 823 |     before "sliding" the two across one another:
 824 | 
 825 |     >>> np.convolve([1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 0.5])
 826 |     array([0. , 1. , 2.5, 4. , 1.5])
 827 | 
 828 |     Only return the middle values of the convolution.
 829 |     Contains boundary effects, where zeros are taken
 830 |     into account:
 831 | 
 832 |     >>> np.convolve([1,2,3],[0,1,0.5], 'same')
 833 |     array([1. ,  2.5,  4. ])
 834 | 
 835 |     The two arrays are of the same length, so there
 836 |     is only one position where they completely overlap:
 837 | 
 838 |     >>> np.convolve([1,2,3],[0,1,0.5], 'valid')
 839 |     array([2.5])
 840 | 
 841 |     """
 842 |     a, v = array(a, copy=False, ndmin=1), array(v, copy=False, ndmin=1)
 843 |     if (len(v) > len(a)):
 844 |         a, v = v, a
 845 |     if len(a) == 0:
 846 |         raise ValueError('a cannot be empty')
 847 |     if len(v) == 0:
 848 |         raise ValueError('v cannot be empty')
 849 |     mode = _mode_from_name(mode)
 850 |     return multiarray.correlate(a, v[::-1], mode)
 851 |
